title: "Onondaga Nation"
subtitle: "United States"
region: "North America"
tags: [ethnography, north-america]

## Overview

The Onondaga people are one of the five original nations of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy in the Northeastern Woodlands. Their historical homelands are in and around present-day Onondaga County, New York, south of Lake Ontario. The Onondaga Nation is located on the Onondaga Reservation south of Nedrow, New York, outside Syracuse; Onondaga people also live near Brantford, Ontario, on Six Nations territory as part of the Bearfoot Onondaga First Nation and Onondaga Clear Sky First Nation. Because of their central position in the Confederacy, they are regarded as the “Keepers of the Fire.” Onondaga is described as the capital of the Haudenosaunee land, and the Onondaga were the Central Fire-Keepers, guardians of the league, and keepers of its law, traditions, and institutions.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name human face motifs in archaeological evidence.

### Clothing & dress

They state that Onondaga funerals were quiet and solemn, with women covering their faces, but provide no further description of the covering or of clothing used in funerary contexts.

### Architecture

Pre-colonial Onondaga villages were continually placed on defensive high points away from rivers, with defensive earthen embankments. The sources also describe continuity of house forms and inferred communal living. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy is figuratively represented by a longhouse that shelters the Five Nations, and ceremonial songs were performed in the longhouse.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Archaeological evidence records a gradual evolution of pottery vessels and smoking pipe forms and decorations, as well as a gradual evolution of stone and bone tools and implements. They also identify Alfred Warner Jacques as a craftsman of traditional wooden lacrosse sticks.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They mention wampum, called *gaswę́hdaʼ*, as an object employed in all matters of public importance and as the medium for public confession of sins.

## Music & performance

Ceremonial songs are performed in the longhouse and danced to in a counter-clockwise direction. This direction is described as the life-providing direction of Mother Earth, moon, and stars. The more spirited the singing and dancing, the more thanks is given to the Creator.

The Onondaga place great emphasis on giving thanks, and ceremonial performance is connected with their ceremonies and lunar calendar. Faith-keepers, called *hona·di·hų́·da*, are responsible for initiating ceremonies according to the different moons. The sources describe dancing and singing as parts of several named observances, including the Planting Feast, the Strawberry Feast, the Green Bean Dance, and the Green Corn dance.

## Dance & theatre

The sources describe dances connected with religious services, feasts, children’s activities, the Thunder, the Four Persons, the Holder of the Heavens, and gambling. The Planting Feast includes one day for the children’s dance and days for the Four Persons, the Holder for the Heavens, the Thunder, and gambling. The Strawberry Feast includes dancing for the Thunder and a feast of strawberries. The Green Bean Dance includes dances for the Thunder and a mixture of war and feather dances. The Green Corn dance follows the Green Bean dance and includes days for religious services, children, the Four Persons, the Holder of the Heavens, and the Thunder.

## Festivals & rituals

The Onondaga ceremonial calendar follows the lunar calendar, with faith-keepers initiating ceremonies according to the different moons. The Planting Feast takes place in May or when the Onondaga believe the ground is ready. It lasts three days for penitential and religious services, followed by a day for the children’s dance and days associated with the Four Persons, the Holder for the Heavens, the Thunder, and gambling.

The Strawberry Feast comes when the berries are ripe. It includes dancing for the Thunder and a feast of strawberries. The Green Bean Dance comes when the green beans are fit for use and includes dances for the Thunder and a mixture of war and feather dances. The Green Corn dance always follows the Green Bean dance and includes religious services, children’s activities, observances for the Four Persons and the Holder of the Heavens, and a feast associated with the Thunder. The Onondaga Thanksgiving feast in October closely resembles the Green Corn Dance.

The sources also describe public confession of sins upon a string of wampum and the sprinkling of ashes in the treatment of the sick. Funerals are described as quiet and solemn, with women covering their faces.

## Foodways

The sources identify several foods and food-related observances. The Strawberry Feast includes a feast of strawberries and takes place when the berries are ripe. The Green Corn dance includes a feast associated with the Thunder. The Planting Feast is connected to the point when the Onondaga believe the ground is ready, while the Green Bean Dance takes place when green beans are fit for use.

Following the Sullivan Expedition and the brutal winter of 1780, a massive swarm of periodical cicadas provided a source of sustenance for Onondaga people experiencing severe food insecurity. The insects emerge from underground every seventeen years. The sudden arrival of the cicadas, specifically Brood VII, also known as the Onondaga brood, is commemorated by the Onondaga as an intervention by the Creator that ensured their survival after the campaigns and winter.

## Oral tradition & literature

According to oral tradition, the Great Peacemaker approached the Onondaga and four other nations to found the Haudenosaunee. The tradition states that the Seneca nation was debating whether to join the Haudenosaunee based on the Great Peacemaker’s teachings when a solar eclipse took place. The most likely eclipse visible in the area is identified as occurring in 1142 AD. Archaeological studies support aspects of the tradition, with carbon dating of particular Onondaga habitation sites showing dates beginning close to 1200 AD ± 60 years and growth for hundreds of years.

The culture hero Hayęhwáthaʼ was Onondaga and was essential in the early organization of the league. The sources also state that Handsome Lake, the Seneca half-brother of Cornplanter and author of his eponymous Code, died at Onondaga.

## Language & religion

The sources identify Onondaga as the language of the Onondaga people and provide several Onondaga terms, including *Onoñdaʼgegáʼ*, meaning “People of the Hills,” and *honatjisdané·daʼ*, meaning “Keepers of the Fire” or the Central Fire-Keepers.

Onondaga ceremonies emphasize giving thanks to the Creator. Ceremonial songs and dances take place in the longhouse, and faith-keepers initiate ceremonies according to the lunar calendar. The sources mention Mother Earth, moon, and stars as connected with the life-providing direction of ceremonial dancing. They also describe the Thunder, the Four Persons, and the Holder of the Heavens as figures associated with ceremonies. The sprinkling of ashes in treating the sick and public confession upon wampum are also documented.

## Sources & further reading

- “Onondaga people,” *Wikipedia*, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onondaga_people
- The sources supplied for this profile contain no UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscriptions for the United States concerning the Onondaga people.
- The sources supplied contain no museum catalogue records for the objects shown.

commons_photos.title: 20220508 - 07 - Cohoes, New York - Tree of Peace at Falls View Park.jpg
commons_photos.description: Located at Falls View Park in Cohoes, New York is this "tree of peace" planted in 2016 in a ceremony held jointly by Brookfield Renewable Power and the Hiawatha Institute for Indigenous Knowledge. It marks the site of one of the formative events in the pre-Columbian history of this region: it was here where Deganawida, a prophet and seer from the Onondaga tribe known by the sobriquet Great Peacemaker, first presented the Great Law of Peace (Gayanashagowa) to the local Mohawk people. This first step in the foundation of the Iroquois Confederacy - which was finalized some years later at a ratification council in Ganondagan, near the town of Victor, New York - occurred at an uncertain date that most scholars place within the rough range of 1200-1450 A.D. The rim of Cohoes Falls is seen in the background just over the top of the stone wall. As seen in May 2022.
